# Tester Exchange: Google Play closed testing guides (full text)

> Source: https://testerexchange.com/. Updated 2026-11-07. The short index is https://testerexchange.com/llms.txt.

---

## How to get 12 testers for Google Play closed testing
URL: https://testerexchange.com/guide/

If you created a personal Google Play developer account after 13 November 2023, you can't publish to production right away. You first need a closed test with at least 12 testers who stay opted in for 14 days in a row. Google also reviews whether those testers actually used your app. This guide walks through the whole process and shows a free way to find real testers.

### The rule: 12 testers × 14 days

Google Play requires new personal developer accounts to run a closed test before applying for production access. The requirement:

- At least 12 testers opted in to your closed testing track
- They stay opted in for at least 14 continuous days
- After that, you apply for production in Play Console and answer questions about your test
- Organization accounts (with a D-U-N-S number) are exempt

The number was 20 testers until December 2024, when Google lowered it to 12. The 14-day clock only counts days with 12 or more testers opted in, so if testers leave and you drop to 11, you lose progress.

### Why apps get rejected after 14 days

Many developers reach 14 days and still get rejected with a message about insufficient testing or engagement. Google looks at whether testers really opened and used the app, not only whether they opted in.

Installs from people who never open the app, or one shared phone with many accounts, don't count as real testing. What helps: testers who open the app regularly during the 14 days, feedback you can describe, and new builds that show you acted on it.

### Set up the closed test in Play Console

1. Open Play Console → your app → Test and release → Testing → Closed testing, and create a track (or use the default Alpha track).
2. Under Testers, choose a Google Group or an email list. A Google Group is easiest: anyone who joins the group can opt in.
3. Upload an app bundle to the track, set the countries, and send the release for review.
4. Once it's approved, copy the opt-in link (https://play.google.com/apps/testing/your.package.name). Testers open it, tap Become a tester, then install from Google Play.
5. Check the Testers tab in Play Console to see how many people have opted in.

### Where to find 12 real testers

- Friends and family. Free, but most people don't have 12 Android users willing to open an app daily for two weeks.
- Test-for-test communities. Developers test each other's apps. Free, and testers understand what's needed. The risk is people who opt in and never open your app.
- Paid tester services. Usually US$10–35 per app. Fast, but you're trusting that the testers are real and active.
- Tester Exchange. A free test-for-test exchange: testers open each app once a day from their phone's browser, every day is recorded, and testers are paid in credits only for the days they actually opened the app.

### How Tester Exchange works

1. Add your app: paste its Google Play link at /start.
2. Choose how to get testers: free (your phone is given apps to test, a minute a day, and each app you test brings a tester to yours) or skip testing with credits (paid apps get testers first).
3. Open testerexchange.com/earn in your Android phone's browser and sign in with Google. There's no app to install.
4. Add your testers to your closed test in Play Console.
5. Testers open your app every day for 14 days, and each day they open it is recorded.
6. After 14 days, open your report: daily active testers, feedback, and draft answers for Play Console's production-access questions.

### Keep testers engaged for 14 days

- Recruit 14–15 testers, not exactly 12, so a few dropouts don't reset your clock.
- Tell testers what to try: one or two concrete tasks, not "please test my app".
- Ship at least one update during the test, and fix what testers report.
- Ask for written feedback. You'll need to summarize it when you apply for production.

### Apply for production access

After 14 days, go to Play Console → Dashboard → Apply for production. Google asks about how you recruited testers, how they engaged with your app, the feedback you received, what you changed, and why the app is ready. Answer with real numbers: how many testers, how many days they used the app, what they reported, and which fixes you shipped. Reviews usually take up to 7 days.

### Frequently asked questions

**Do the 12 testers need to use the app every day?** Google requires them to stay opted in for 14 days and reviews engagement. Regular real use is what avoids an "insufficient testing" rejection.

**Can I use my own phones or accounts as testers?** Google can tell when many accounts share one device, and it doesn't count as real testing. Use real people on their own phones.

**Does a tester who leaves reset the 14 days?** The count only advances on days with at least 12 opted-in testers. Recruit a couple of extra testers so dropouts don't stall you.

**Is Tester Exchange free?** Yes. Testing is free: each app you test on your phone brings a tester to yours. New members get free starting credits. Buying credits is optional and lets you skip testing; paid apps get testers first.

## Google Play 12 testers for apps made with App Inventor, Kodular, Flutter, Unity and other builders
URL: https://testerexchange.com/guide/12-testers-app-builders/

It doesn't matter which tool you used to build your app. If your Google Play developer account is a new personal account, you need a closed test with at least 12 testers for 14 days before you can publish to production. This guide covers the parts that trip up builder and game-engine users, and a free way to find the testers.

### The rule is the same for every tool

Google checks your developer account, not your tool. Apps made with MIT App Inventor, Kodular, Niotron, Sketchware, Thunkable, FlutterFlow, Flutter, React Native, Expo, Unity or Godot all go through the same closed test.

If you created a personal developer account after 13 November 2023, you need at least 12 testers opted in for 14 days in a row before you can apply for production access. Organization accounts don't have this requirement.

### Step 1: export a release build your builder can sign

1. Export an Android App Bundle (.aab). Google Play needs an .aab for new apps. Most builders and engines can export one; if yours only offers an APK, check its documentation for the App Bundle option.
2. Keep your signing key safe. Builders such as App Inventor and Kodular create a keystore for you. Download a backup of it. You need the same key for every update.
3. Choose your package name carefully. It can never change once the app is on Google Play.
4. Meet the target API level. Google Play only accepts builds that target a recent Android version. If the upload is rejected for its target API level, update your builder or engine and export again.

### Step 2: set up the closed test

1. In Play Console, open Test and release → Testing → Closed testing and create a track.
2. Add testers with a Google Group rather than an email list: testers join the group themselves, and you never paste emails again.
3. Upload your .aab to the closed track, add release notes and send it for review.
4. Copy the opt-in link. Testers join the group, open the opt-in link, tap "Become a tester", then install from Google Play.

### Step 3: find 12 testers who stay for 14 days

Twelve names on a list isn't enough. Google reviews whether testers really used your app, and the 14 days only count while at least 12 testers are opted in. Recruit 14 or 15 people, so one or two dropouts don't stop the clock.

- Friends and family with Android phones: free, but they often stop opening the app after a few days.
- Builder communities and forums: fellow builders understand the rule, and many swap tests.
- A test exchange: on Tester Exchange you open other developers' apps in your phone's browser, about a minute a day, and each day you test earns credits toward testers for your own app.

### Step 4: keep testers active and ship an update

- Give testers one small task per day, so they have a reason to open the app.
- Upload a new build with fixes around day 7 and say what changed. Builders make this quick: export, upload to the same closed track, done.
- Ask for written feedback and fix what you can. It also gives you real answers for the production questions.

### Step 5: apply for production

After 14 days, apply for production access in the Play Console dashboard. Google asks how you recruited testers, how they used the app and what you changed based on their feedback. Answer with real numbers from your test. Google usually replies within about a week.

### Frequently asked questions

**Do apps made with App Inventor or Kodular need 12 testers too?** Yes. The requirement depends on your developer account, not the tool. New personal accounts need 12 testers opted in for 14 days, whatever the app was built with.

**Can my testers install an APK I send them instead?** No. Only installs from the closed test on Google Play count. Testers must opt in with the link from Play Console and install from the Play Store.

**Do I need a new build to start the closed test?** You need at least one build uploaded to the closed track. Uploading a second build during the test with fixes from tester feedback is a good idea.

**Is there a free way to get 12 testers?** Yes. Test swaps are free: you test other developers' apps and they test yours. On Tester Exchange each day a tester opens your app is recorded, so you can see who is really testing.

## Fix "app not available" for Google Play closed testers
URL: https://testerexchange.com/guide/app-not-available-for-testers/

Your testers open the link and Google Play says the app isn't available, can't be found, or isn't compatible. Every day this lasts is a day your 14-day clock isn't running. Almost always the cause is one of a handful of setup problems, and you can check them all in about ten minutes. Work through this list in order.

### Quick checklist

- Is the release on the closed track Published, not In review or Draft?
- Is the tester's email (or your Google Group) on that same closed track?
- Did the tester open the opt-in link and tap to become a tester?
- Is the tester signed in to Google Play with that same Google Account?
- Is the tester's country selected for the app?
- Does the tester's phone meet your minimum Android version and device requirements?
- Has it been a few hours since the first publish?
- Is the tester also opted into your internal test?

### 1. The track isn't published yet

Google says the opt-in link displays only when the app status is Published. If your first closed release is still in review, or saved but never sent for review, testers will see nothing useful.

Open Publishing overview. If there are changes waiting to be sent, send them. If managed publishing is on, approved changes wait until you click Publish. Also check the Inbox and Policy status pages for rejections.

### 2. It was published minutes ago

Google notes that after the first publish the test link can take several hours to become available, and later changes can also take several hours. If everything else is right, wait half a day before changing anything. Changing settings repeatedly can trigger new reviews and add delay.

### 3. The tester isn't on the track

Being invited is not the same as being on the track. Open Test and release, then Testing, then Closed testing, then Manage track, then Testers. Make sure the email list with the tester's address is ticked for this track and saved, or that your Google Group address is entered under Google Groups.

With a Google Group, the tester also has to be a member of the group before opting in. Google says only members of the specified groups can join the test. If you use Tester Exchange, the group to add is testerexchange-testers@googlegroups.com, and we add our testers to it.

### 4. Wrong Google Account on the phone

This is the most common cause with friends and family. The tester gave you their work email, or the phone has two Google Accounts and the Play Store is using the other one.

Ask the tester to open the Play Store, tap their profile picture and check which account is active. The opt-in link must be opened while signed in to the account on your list, in the same browser profile. Then they install from the Play Store on the phone with that account. If needed, add their other address to your list too.

### 5. The tester never opted in

Each tester must open the opt-in link and accept, one by one. Sending them the Play Store link alone isn't enough. After they accept, Google shows a link to download the app from Google Play. Testers can't find a closed test by searching the Play Store.

### 6. Country or device not supported

If the tester's country isn't in your Countries / regions list, the app won't be available to them. Add the country; Google says country changes apply across all tracks.

"Your device isn't compatible" usually means your minimum SDK, required features (for example a camera or specific CPU architecture) or device exclusions rule out that phone. Check the Device catalog in Play Console. Games built only for 64-bit ARM, or with high minimum Android versions, often hit this.

### 7. They're in your internal test

Google says users who opt into internal testing aren't eligible for open and closed testing. If a tester joined your internal test earlier, they must leave it first (open the internal opt-in link and leave the program), then opt into the closed test.

### 8. Play Store is showing an old state

If all of the above is right, ask the tester to close the Play Store, clear its cache in Android Settings, and try again. Opening the opt-in link in Chrome on the phone rather than inside another app's built-in browser also helps.

### Protect your 14 days while you fix it

The requirement counts 12 testers opted in continuously for 14 days, so testers who can't get in don't help. Recruit a few extra (15 is a good target) so one stuck tester doesn't delay the whole test. Tester Exchange replaces testers who stop, and its setup screen tells you exactly which Play Console step to take if our testers can't install your app.

### Frequently asked questions

**Why does the Play Store say "item not found"?** Usually the release isn't published yet, the tester is signed in with a different Google Account, or they aren't on the track's email list or Google Group.

**How long after publishing can testers install?** Google says the first test link can take several hours to become available.

**Do testers who can't install count toward 12?** Only opted-in testers count. Someone who never managed to opt in doesn't help your 14 days.

**Can testers find my app by searching Google Play?** No. Closed tests don't appear in search. Share the opt-in link or the Play Store link.

**Do I need to republish after adding testers?** Adding emails to a list or members to a Google Group doesn't need a new release. Save the Testers tab changes and send them if Publishing overview asks.

## Automate Google Play closed testing with AI agents
URL: https://testerexchange.com/guide/automate-closed-testing-with-ai-agents/

If you already ship code with an AI agent, you can hand it most of the busywork of Google Play's closed testing requirement too: listing your app, recruiting testers, checking progress and pulling numbers for the production access form. Tester Exchange has an MCP server, a one-endpoint HTTP API and an A2A agent card for this. This guide shows how to connect Claude Code, Claude Desktop, Cursor and other clients, what to ask, and the parts no agent can do for you.

### What an agent can and can't do

Google requires personal developer accounts created after 13 November 2023 to run a closed test with at least 12 testers opted in for 14 continuous days before applying for production. Most of the work around that is coordination, which agents handle well.

- An agent can: add your app, open a tester campaign, apply your credits, check how many testers are active, pause or close a campaign, fetch the daily-activity report and help draft production access answers from it.
- A human must: add the testers' Google Group to the closed track in Play Console, publish the release, pay for credits (checkout always happens in a person's browser) and click Apply for production.
- Nobody can automate: the 14 days of real use. That is done by real people on their own Android phones, which is the whole point of Google's rule.

### 1. Create a token

1. Sign in at https://testerexchange.com/api.
2. Create a personal token. It starts with tx_. Copy it now and store it like a password.
3. Tokens can be revoked at any time. A token can spend credits on campaigns, but it can't pay, withdraw money or delete your account.

### 2. Connect the MCP server

The MCP server uses Streamable HTTP at https://vvrlxzbngxfxddywidoq.supabase.co/functions/v1/mcp. Send your token in the header Authorization: Bearer tx_YOUR_TOKEN.

Claude Code: run this once in your terminal.

claude mcp add --transport http tester-exchange https://vvrlxzbngxfxddywidoq.supabase.co/functions/v1/mcp --header "Authorization: Bearer tx_YOUR_TOKEN"

Claude Desktop, Cursor, VS Code and other clients with a JSON config: add a server named tester-exchange with type http, the URL above, and a headers entry with Authorization set to Bearer tx_YOUR_TOKEN. The exact config file location depends on your client; check its MCP documentation.

Clients that only take a URL (some ChatGPT and web connectors): the docs at https://testerexchange.com/agents/ list a URL form for them. Without a token, the public tools (what Tester Exchange is, pricing, platform stats) still work.

### 3. The one tool to start with: get_testers

You don't need to learn the whole tool list. The main tool is get_testers(package_name, name?). One call adds your app, opens its test, applies your credits and returns your progress plus the steps only a human can do, such as adding the Google Group in Play Console. Call it again any time to check progress.

Other tools cover the details: my_apps, campaign_report (testers, daily activity, feedback and production-access data), add_testers, set_campaign_status (pause, resume or close; unused credits go back to your balance), share_kit and buy_credits_links, which returns checkout links for a human to pay.

### Prompts that work

- "Get 15 testers for com.example.app and tell me what I need to do in Play Console."
- "Check my Tester Exchange campaign for com.example.app. How many testers were active each day this week?"
- "Pull the campaign report and draft my production access answers. Use only the real numbers."
- "Close the campaign for com.example.app now that production access is approved."

Ask for 15 testers rather than 12, so a dropout can't take you under Google's minimum.

### HTTP API for scripts and CI

If your tool doesn't speak MCP, use the HTTP endpoint: POST https://vvrlxzbngxfxddywidoq.supabase.co/rest/v1/rpc/agent_call. The body is JSON with p_token (your tx_ token), p_action (for example help, my_apps or start_campaign) and p_args (for example a package_name and a tester count). Send the public apikey header shown in the docs.

Call the help action first: it returns every action and its arguments. The full schema is at https://testerexchange.com/openapi.json, which works with ChatGPT custom GPT actions and other OpenAPI tools.

### A2A agent card

For agent-to-agent setups, Tester Exchange publishes an A2A agent card at https://testerexchange.com/.well-known/agent-card.json. Orchestrators that support the A2A protocol can discover what the agent offers and how to call it. Use the same tx_ token for anything tied to your account.

### A full run, start to finish

1. You upload your first .aab to the closed track in Play Console.
2. Your agent calls get_testers for your package name and tells you to add testerexchange-testers@googlegroups.com under Google Groups on the closed track.
3. You add the group, save, and make sure the release is published.
4. If you lack credits, the agent gives you a checkout link. You pay ($12.99 for 12 testers, $14.99 for 15, $22.99 for 25) or earn credits free by testing other apps at https://testerexchange.com/earn.
5. Real testers install and use your app for 14 days. Your agent checks progress daily and warns you if active testers fall.
6. On day 15, the agent pulls the campaign report and drafts your production access answers. You review them and click Apply for production.

### Safety notes

- Keep tokens out of git. Put them in your client's secret store or an environment variable.
- Tokens are stored only as hashes on our side and are limited to 10 per account. Revoke any token you no longer use.
- Read what the agent writes in your production form before you submit. Google asks you to describe your test truthfully.

### Frequently asked questions

**Can an AI agent complete the 14-day test for me?** No. The 14 days need real people using your app on their own phones. Agents handle setup, monitoring and reporting.

**Can the agent pay for testers?** No. It can return checkout links, but payment always happens in a human's browser.

**Which clients work with the MCP server?** Any client that supports remote MCP over Streamable HTTP with a custom header, including Claude Code, Claude Desktop, Cursor and VS Code. Others can use the HTTP API.

**Where do I get a token?** At https://testerexchange.com/api after signing in. Tokens start with tx_ and can be revoked at any time.

**Does the agent change anything in my Play Console?** No. It has no access to your Play Console. It tells you the steps to do there.

## The best way to get 12 testers for Google Play closed testing
URL: https://testerexchange.com/guide/best-way-to-get-12-testers/

Short answer: if you have time and no budget, join a free tester exchange and test other developers' apps. If you want it done and don't want to spend a few hours a week testing, pay a service that shows daily proof of use. Fiverr gigs are the cheapest to start but the hardest to check. Google requires 12 testers opted in continuously for 14 days for personal developer accounts created after 13 November 2023; it does not say where the testers must come from. This page compares the four common routes. Details on competitors come from their own public pages in November 2026 and can change.

### Quick comparison

Costs are one-time per app unless noted.

- Free exchange (Tester Exchange free testing, Testers Community app): $0. You test other developers' apps and earn credits toward testers for yours. Cost is your time, about a minute a day per app. Speed depends on how many developers are active.
- Paid service (Tester Exchange, Testers Community paid plan): Tester Exchange charges $12.99 for 12 testers, $14.99 for 15 or $22.99 for 25. Testers Community lists its paid plan from $15. Testers start within hours to a day or two.
- Fiverr or Freelancer gig: gig pages we looked at list prices up to about $50 for 12 testers and two weeks of delivery. Quality varies by seller and is hard to verify.
- Reddit, Discord, Telegram and "test for test" posts: $0, but you chase every tester yourself and many drop out before day 14.

### Free exchanges: how they work

In a free exchange every developer is also a tester. Testers Community describes a credit system where you test three apps to earn credits, then spend them to get testers for yours, and groups developers into packs that run together for about two weeks. On Tester Exchange you open other developers' apps each day and earn credits; developers who test others get testers for their own app sooner.

Free exchanges work best when you start early, because you earn testers by testing and the 14 days only start once all your testers are in. Expect to open each assigned app once a day.

On Tester Exchange the daily step is one tap per app in your phone's browser; no extra app is needed.

### Paid services: what to check

Paying is allowed by Google's stated rule, but the test only helps if the testers are real people who stay opted in. Before you pay, check that testers use real phones, that spare testers replace dropouts, and that you get daily proof of use rather than only a promise.

Refund terms differ. Testers Community says it refunds if Google rejects the app after its cycle. Tester Exchange purchases are final: credits do not convert back to money, and unused credits stay on your balance.

### Fiverr and other freelance gigs

Hundreds of sellers offer 12 or 20 testers for 14 days, usually with a Google Play questionnaire helper. Ratings and order counts help, but you usually cannot see whether testers opened your app each day. Ask the seller how many distinct real devices they use and whether you get daily proof.

### Which one should you pick?

1. No budget and at least three weeks before your launch date: join a free exchange today and keep testing other apps for all 14 days.
2. Some budget and a deadline: pay for a service with daily proof and replacement of dropouts, and ask for 15 testers so a few dropouts don't reset your count.
3. Already have friends and family on Android: invite them first, then fill the remaining seats from an exchange or a paid pack.
4. Rejected before with "more testing required": fix the engagement problem first. See the guide on insufficient testing engagement.

### How many testers should you ask for?

Google's minimum is 12, and every tester must stay opted in for 14 days in a row. Ask for 15 or more so a few dropouts don't leave you below 12 on day 10.

### Frequently asked questions

**What is the cheapest way to get 12 testers for Google Play?** A free tester exchange costs nothing but your time: you test other developers' apps and they test yours. Paid options start around $13 for 12 testers.

**Is a free tester exchange as good as paying?** It can be, if enough developers are active and you keep testing for all 14 days. Paying is faster and takes less of your time.

**Are Fiverr testers safe to use?** Quality varies a lot. Ask for proof of real devices and daily use. Google's requirement is that testers are opted in continuously for 14 days; it asks you to describe the test truthfully in the production access form.

**How many testers should I get?** Ask for 15 or more. Twelve is the minimum, and dropouts below 12 can break the 14 days.

**Does Tester Exchange offer refunds?** No. Purchases are final and credits do not convert back to money; unused credits stay on your balance.

## Closed testing for games on Google Play: a guide for Unity, Unreal and Godot
URL: https://testerexchange.com/guide/closed-testing-for-games/

Games go through the same closed testing requirement as any other app: if your personal developer account was created after 13 November 2023, you need at least 12 testers opted in for 14 days in a row before you can apply for production. Games have their own pitfalls, though: big downloads, devices that can't run the build, and testers who open the game once and never come back. This guide covers what game developers should set up and what to ask testers to do.

### The same rule, with game-specific risks

Google treats games and apps alike here. Run a closed test with at least 12 testers who stay opted in continuously for 14 days, then apply for production. The production form asks about tester engagement, feedback and what you changed, so a test where nobody played past the tutorial makes for weak answers.

The risks that hit games more than other apps:

- Device compatibility: testers see "your device isn't compatible" and can't install.
- Download size: a large first download on mobile data puts testers off.
- Session length: people won't play a 20-minute level every day for two weeks.
- Content gaps: a vertical slice with one level runs out of things to do by day three.

### Build settings to check first

- Unity: build an Android App Bundle (.aab), use IL2CPP with ARM64 enabled (Google Play requires 64-bit support), and set a minimum API level that doesn't exclude more phones than you need to. If your build is large, use Play Asset Delivery rather than one huge download.
- Unreal Engine: package for Android as an App Bundle with arm64, check the target and minimum SDK levels in Project Settings, and keep the first download small by moving optional content into asset packs.
- Godot: use the Android export template with Gradle build enabled and export as AAB. Make sure arm64-v8a is included, and test the renderer on a low-end phone, because some devices handle the Compatibility renderer better than Forward+ or Mobile.
- All engines: target the API level Google Play currently requires for new apps, and sign with Play App Signing.

After uploading, open the Device catalog in Play Console to see how many devices your build supports. If a big share is excluded, fix it before testers arrive.

### Set up the test

1. Create or open the closed track: Test and release, then Testing, then Closed testing.
2. Add countries where your testers live.
3. Add testers with an email list or a Google Group. With Tester Exchange, add testerexchange-testers@googlegroups.com.
4. Upload the .aab, send the release for review and wait until it shows Published.
5. Share the opt-in link. The first time, it can take several hours to start working.

If testers report "app not available", see the guide on fixing that. It covers wrong accounts, countries and unpublished tracks.

### What to ask testers to play

Give testers small daily goals that fit into a couple of minutes. Real, varied play is what helps you, and it's what you'll describe later in the production form.

- Days 1 to 3: finish the tutorial and the first level. Report anything confusing.
- Days 4 to 7: play one short session a day; try settings, sound, controls and pausing.
- Days 8 to 11: try a new build with fixes; replay a level to see if it feels better.
- Days 12 to 14: play the hardest content available and report crashes, lag or battery drain.

If your game has daily rewards, a short daily challenge or a quick mode, point testers at it. It fits the daily rhythm naturally.

### Show engagement

- Ship at least one update during the test, ideally two. Fixing a reported crash is the best story for the production form.
- Use Android vitals and the pre-launch report in Play Console to find crashes and ANRs on real devices.
- Collect written feedback in a simple form: device model, what they did, what happened.
- Keep a log of daily active testers, sessions, bugs found and builds shipped.

### Multiplayer and online games

If your game needs a server, keep it running for all 14 days, and make sure the game is still playable when testers are alone. A lobby that never fills looks like an empty test. Add bots or a solo mode for the test period if you can.

If you need sign-in, give testers a working guest mode or clear instructions. Sign-in walls lose testers on day one.

### Getting enough players

Ask for 15 testers rather than 12, because some players drop out of games quickly. Tester Exchange sends real people who play on their own Android phones and shows daily use for each tester: $12.99 for 12, $14.99 for 15 or $22.99 for 25, paid once. You can also earn testers free by testing other developers' apps and games at https://testerexchange.com/earn.

### Frequently asked questions

**Do games need closed testing too?** Yes. The requirement applies to all apps from personal accounts created after 13 November 2023, including games.

**Can my game still be unfinished during closed testing?** Yes, a closed test is for a work in progress. But testers need enough content to play for two weeks, and you should keep improving it during the test.

**Why can't some testers install my game?** Usually device compatibility: a high minimum Android version, missing 64-bit support, or required hardware features. Check the Device catalog in Play Console.

**How long should testers play each day?** Google doesn't set a number. A short real session every day is better than one long session and then nothing.

**Should I use Play Asset Delivery for the test?** If your game is large, yes. Smaller first downloads mean more testers actually install and start playing.

## Does the 14-day closed test reset when testers drop out?
URL: https://testerexchange.com/guide/does-14-day-closed-test-reset/

Short answer: one tester leaving doesn't reset anything by itself, but falling below 12 opted-in testers does break your progress. Google counts testers who have been opted in continuously, so the people who leave, and the people who replace them, change the math. This guide explains how the count works according to Google's Help Center, what to do mid-test, and why 15 is the number to aim for.

### What Google actually counts

Google's requirement for personal accounts created after 13 November 2023 is a closed test with at least 12 testers who have been opted in continuously for at least 14 days. Three details in Google's wording matter here:

- The 14 days must be consecutive. There is no pausing and resuming.
- Testers who opt in, test for fewer than 14 days and then opt out don't count toward the requirement.
- At least 12 testers must be opted in when you apply for production access.

Think of it per tester: each person has their own clock that starts when they opt in. You qualify when at least 12 people have each been opted in for 14 days in a row, and are still opted in.

### Common scenarios

- You had 15, one leaves on day 8. The other 14 keep counting. On day 14 you still have 14 qualifying testers. No problem.
- You had exactly 12, one leaves on day 8. Now only 11 people can reach 14 days. You need a replacement, and that person's 14 days start on the day they opt in. Your earliest apply date moves back about a week.
- A tester opts out and back in. Google says opting out and back in restarts that tester's consecutive count.
- A tester stays opted in but stops opening the app. They still count toward 12 for the opt-in rule, but they hurt you on engagement, which Google asks about in the production form.
- A tester uninstalls the app but doesn't opt out. They are probably still opted in, but they aren't testing. Treat them like the previous case.

### Why ask for 15 testers, not 12

Dropouts are normal. People change phones, forget, run out of storage or lose interest. With exactly 12, any single dropout before day 14 pushes your apply date back. With 15, you can lose three people and still apply on time.

It also helps engagement. Google looks at how testers used the app. If three of fifteen are quiet, the other twelve still show steady use. If three of twelve are quiet, a quarter of your test looks inactive.

On Tester Exchange, 15 testers cost $14.99 compared with $12.99 for 12, which is cheap insurance against an extra week of waiting.

### What to do mid-test

1. Check the opted-in tester count in Play Console every two or three days.
2. If you see a drop, add replacements at once. Every day you wait is a day added to their 14.
3. Message quiet testers with one concrete task ("try the new search screen in build 1.0.3") rather than a general reminder.
4. Ship an update during the test. A fresh build gives testers a reason to open the app again.
5. Don't apply until you have at least 12 testers who have each passed 14 consecutive days and are still opted in. A margin of two or three is safer.

### Things that don't reset your progress

- Uploading new builds to the same closed track. Testers stay opted in and get the update.
- Adding more testers. New people start their own 14 days; existing testers keep theirs.
- Editing the store listing or release notes.

Things to avoid: removing the email list or Google Group from the track, or deleting the track. Testers may lose access, and it's unclear how Google then treats their opt-in, so don't risk it.

### How Tester Exchange handles dropouts

On Tester Exchange, testers are real people on their own Android phones and you see daily use for each one. If a tester stops, a new one takes the seat, and you only pay for days testers actually open your app. Unused credits stay on your balance. You can pay once for 12, 15 or 25 testers, or get testers free by testing other developers' apps at https://testerexchange.com/earn in your phone's browser.

### Frequently asked questions

**If one tester leaves, does my 14 days start over?** Not for the others. Each tester's clock is separate. You only lose time if you fall below 12 testers who can complete 14 consecutive days.

**Does a replacement tester start at day 1?** Yes. Their 14 consecutive days start when they opt in.

**What if a tester opts out by mistake and rejoins?** Google says opting out and back in restarts their consecutive count.

**Do inactive testers count?** If they stay opted in, they count toward the 12. But low engagement is a common reason Google asks for more testing.

**How many spare testers should I have?** Aim for 15 in total, three above Google's minimum.

## Earn money testing Android apps: an honest guide
URL: https://testerexchange.com/guide/earn-money-testing-android-apps/

Developers with new Google Play accounts need real people to test their apps for 14 days before they can publish. You can be one of those people from your Android phone's browser at https://testerexchange.com/earn, with no extra app to install. You get paid a small amount for each test you finish. Let's be clear up front: this is pocket money, not an income. This guide explains how it works, what you have to do, and how much you can realistically expect.

### Why developers need testers

Google requires personal developer accounts created after 13 November 2023 to run a closed test with at least 12 testers who stay opted in for 14 days in a row before the app can go public. Many solo developers don't know 12 Android users who will do that, so they look for testers.

Google also checks whether testers actually used the app. That's why the work is simple but needs to be real: open the app and use it, every day, on your own phone.

### What you earn

- US$0.50 for each finished 14-day test on an app marked 💵. These are paying customers' apps that still need testers. Other apps earn credits, which get testers for your own app.
- Cash out from US$3. That's six finished tests.
- Payout methods: PayPal, Binance Pay or Payoneer.

You can be in several tests at the same time, because each one only takes a minute or two a day. How many cash apps you get depends on how many paying customers need testers that week. If five of your tests pay cash, you might earn US$2.50 in about two weeks. Treat it as a small bonus for a few minutes a day, not a job.

### How it works, step by step

1. On your Android phone, open https://testerexchange.com/earn in your browser and sign in.
2. Your list of apps fills itself. Tap the green button: the first time, it asks you to join the testers group (once), then to become a tester on Google Play.
3. Install the app from Google Play through the test link.
4. Open the app and actually use it for a minute or two every day for 14 days. Try the main features, and send feedback if something breaks or confuses you.
5. Stay in the test for all 14 days. Don't leave the test or uninstall the app early.
6. When a test on a 💵 app is finished, US$0.50 is added to your balance. Cash out once you reach US$3.

### The rules

- Real phone only. Use your own Android phone. Emulators, cloud phones and device farms are not allowed.
- One account per person. Don't create extra accounts or use family members' accounts to collect more tests.
- Use the app for real. Opening and closing it instantly doesn't help the developer and isn't real testing.
- Finish what you start. Leaving early can hurt the developer, because Google counts testers who stay opted in for 14 continuous days.
- Don't leave public reviews for test versions. Google doesn't allow public reviews of test builds anyway; send feedback to the developer instead.

Accounts that break these rules may be removed from testing. The rules exist because developers are relying on you to be a real tester.

### How to be a good tester

- Set a daily reminder at the same time, for example with your morning coffee.
- Spend a minute on a different screen each day, not just the opening screen.
- Write short, specific feedback: what you did, what you expected, what happened.
- Keep the apps until the 14 days are over, even if you don't love them.

### Is it safe?

You install apps from Google Play, not from random files, so they go through Google's normal protections. You don't need to install any Tester Exchange app; everything runs in your browser. Still, use common sense: don't give a test app permissions it obviously doesn't need, and don't enter real payment details or sensitive personal information into an app you're testing.

### Who this is for

It suits people who already spend time on their phone and like trying new apps, students who want a little extra, and developers who want testers for their own app. Developers can test other apps free in exchange for testers on theirs, which is often worth more than the cash.

If you need real income, this isn't it. The pay is small and depends on how many tests are open. But it's honest, flexible and takes very little time.

### Frequently asked questions

**How much can I earn testing apps?** US$0.50 for each finished 14-day test on an app marked 💵, and credits on the others. Running several tests at once, most people earn a few dollars a month.

**What is the minimum payout?** US$3, paid to PayPal, Binance Pay or Payoneer.

**Do I need to install a Tester Exchange app?** No. You use https://testerexchange.com/earn in your Android phone's browser. You only install the apps you test, from Google Play.

**Can I use an iPhone?** No. These are Google Play closed tests, so you need an Android phone with a Google Account.

**Can I have two accounts?** No. One account per person, on a real phone.

**What if I stop before day 14?** The test isn't finished, so it doesn't pay. It also hurts the developer, so only join tests you plan to finish.

## How to get 12 testers for Google Play closed testing for free
URL: https://testerexchange.com/guide/free-closed-testing-testers/

New personal developer accounts must run a closed test with at least 12 testers for 14 days before they can apply for production. You don't have to pay for that. Here are the realistic ways to find 12 testers, what each one costs you in money or time, and what makes testers actually count when Google reviews your test.

### Your options and their trade-offs

Every option below can get you to 12 names on a list. The real question is whether those 12 people will still be opening your app on day 10, because Google looks at how the app was used, not just who opted in.

- Friends and family: free and trustworthy, but few people have 12 friends with Android phones who will open an unfinished app every day for two weeks. Expect a lot of reminding.
- Developer communities and test-for-test swaps: free, and other developers understand the rule. The catch is coordination: you test their apps in return, and informal swaps often fade after a few days with nobody keeping track.
- Paid tester services: fast, typically about US$10–35 per app. The risk is testers who opt in but never really open the app, which is exactly what Google flags. Ask how daily use is checked before you pay.
- Cheap freelance gigs: the lowest price, the highest risk. Fake or inactive accounts and many accounts on one shared device are common, and Google checks engagement, so these testers may not count at all.

### Tester Exchange: pay once, or test for free

Tester Exchange gives you three ways to fill your 12 seats, and you can mix them.

- Bring your own testers: share your app's link with friends and family. They test in their phone's browser with one tap a day, and each of their days is recorded, so you can see who is keeping up.
- Free testing: open other developers' apps in your phone's browser, about a minute a day. Each day you test earns credits toward testers for your own app.
- Pay once: buy 12, 15 or 25 testers. Paid apps get testers before anyone else.
- Daily use you can see: each day a tester opens your app is recorded on your app page, so you know who is actually testing.

### How to choose

- You have 12+ reliable Android friends: use them, give them a daily task, and keep reminding.
- You have time but no budget: join a swap. A structured one with tracking beats a loose chat thread.
- You consider paying: only pay for testers whose daily use is checked, and never for installs alone.
- Whatever you pick: recruit 14–15 testers, not exactly 12, so a few dropouts don't stop the clock.

### Checklist: what makes testers count

- Real people: one person per account, not spare accounts you created yourself.
- Their own phones: each tester uses their own Android device, not one phone shared by many accounts.
- Regular use for the full 14 days: testers open the app regularly from day 1 to day 14, not just once after installing.
- Feedback: testers tell you what broke or confused them, and you ship fixes during the test.

None of this guarantees production access. Google makes the final decision, but a test that ticks every box gives you the strongest case.

### Frequently asked questions

**Can I really get 12 testers for free?** Yes. Friends, developer communities and test exchanges cost nothing but time. On Tester Exchange testing is free, and credits are only for skipping it.

**Are paid tester services worth it?** Only if they can show that testers actually open your app every day. Testers who opt in and never use the app are the most common reason a closed test doesn't pass.

**Do testers from swaps count for Google?** They count like any other tester if they are real people using their own phones and opening your app regularly for the full 14 days.

**How much time does the free exchange take?** You open each app you're given for about 30 seconds a day for 14 days. It's a small daily habit, and it's what gets your own app its testers.

**Does a good closed test guarantee production access?** No. Google decides. Real, active testers and honest answers in the production questionnaire give you the best chance.

## Using friends and family as your 12 Google Play testers
URL: https://testerexchange.com/guide/friends-family-closed-testers/

Google Play's closed-testing rule for new personal developer accounts asks for at least 12 testers who stay opted in for 14 days in a row. Friends and family are allowed, and they are the most trustworthy testers you will find. The hard part is not asking them; it's getting every one of them to keep opening an unfinished app for two weeks. Here is how to make that work, and what to do when you only have five friends with Android phones.

### Can friends and family be closed testers?

Yes. Google doesn't say who your testers must be. What it reviews is whether real people opted in, installed the app from the closed track and used it during the test. A friend on their own Android phone counts exactly like a stranger.

- Each tester needs their own Google account on the phone they use, opted in through your Google Group or email list.
- Their own device: five accounts on one phone is the pattern that looks fake. One person, one phone.
- Installed from Google Play: testers must install from the opt-in link, not from an APK you send them.
- Opted in for all 14 days: someone who leaves the test on day 9 no longer counts toward the 12.

### How to invite them in a way that works

- Ask for 14–15 people, not 12. Someone always loses their phone, changes accounts or forgets.
- Use a Google Group. Friends join with one click, and you never paste emails into Play Console again.
- Send one message with every step: join the group, open the opt-in link, install from Google Play, open the app once a day.
- Check for iPhones first. Many friends don't have an Android phone; ask before you count them.

### Keeping friends active for 14 days

Friends mean well and still forget by day four. Give them a reason and a reminder to open the app every day.

- A tiny daily task: "tap one thing and tell me if it was confusing" beats "please test my app".
- Automatic reminders: testers get a daily email with the apps they still need to open that day.
- A progress view for you: you see who is on day 6 and who stopped, so you know whom to nudge before the clock resets.
- Ship an update in week two: it gives everyone a new reason to open the app and shows Google an active test.

### When you don't have 12 friends

Most developers have three to eight people they can ask. You don't need to find the rest among strangers on forums.

- Free testing: on Tester Exchange you get other developers' apps to open each day, and every day you test earns credits toward testers for yours.
- Skip testing: credits cover the seats your friends leave open, and paid apps get testers first. Members earn credits by testing, or you can buy a small pack.
- Same rules for everyone: every tester, friend or not, is a real person on their own phone, and every day they open your app is recorded the same way.

### Frequently asked questions

**Do friends and family count as testers for Google Play?** Yes, as long as each one uses their own Google account on their own Android phone, installs from your closed-testing opt-in link and stays opted in for the full 14 days.

**Can I use my own second account or my partner's phone with several accounts?** Don't. Several accounts on one device, or accounts you made yourself, look like fake testers. One person, one account, one phone.

**How often do friends need to open the app?** Google doesn't publish a number, but regular use across the whole test is what it looks for. Ask for a short session every day so that a few missed days don't matter.

**What if only five friends can help?** Use them, then fill the other seats from the exchange. On Tester Exchange friends join free through your share link, and the exchange fills the rest.

**Does a test with friends guarantee production access?** No. Google decides. Real, active testers and honest answers in the production-access questions give you the best chance.

## Google Group or email list for your closed test?
URL: https://testerexchange.com/guide/google-group-vs-email-list/

Every closed testing track needs a list of who may install the app. Play Console gives you two options: an email list you manage in Play Console, or a Google Group. Both work for the 12-tester requirement. The difference is how much work it is to add people.

### Quick comparison

- Google Group: anyone with the group link can join, so you don't have to add people one by one. Best when testers come from many places.
- Email list: you paste each tester's Google account email into Play Console. Full control over who gets in, but you have to keep it updated as people join.

### Set up a Google Group

1. Go to groups.google.com and create a group. Set "Who can join" to anyone on the web, so testers don't wait for approval.
2. In Play Console → Testing → Closed testing → your track → Testers, choose Google Groups and add the group's email address.
3. Share two links with testers: the group link (join first) and the opt-in link (become a tester).
4. Testers install the app from Google Play with the same Google account they used to join the group.

### Set up an email list

1. In Play Console → Testing → Closed testing → your track → Testers, create an email list.
2. Paste the Google account emails of your testers, separated by commas, and save.
3. Share the opt-in link. Testers must open it while signed in with the email you added.

### Mistakes that stop testers from seeing your app

- The tester joined with one Google account but their phone's Play Store uses another.
- The group requires approval, so testers are stuck waiting.
- The tester joined the group but never opened the opt-in link and tapped "Become a tester".
- The release isn't approved yet. Testers can't install until the closed track is live.

### Frequently asked questions

**Do group members count toward the 12 testers?** Only people who opted in through the opt-in link count, whichever list type you use.

**Can I use both?** Yes. A track can have email lists and Google Groups at the same time.

**Can testers stay anonymous?** With a Google Group you never need to collect emails yourself. With an email list you need each tester's Google account email.

## Google Play closed testing requirements: the complete 2026 guide
URL: https://testerexchange.com/guide/google-play-closed-testing-requirements/

If you opened a personal Google Play developer account after 13 November 2023, you can't publish straight to production. Google first wants a closed test with at least 12 testers who stay opted in for at least 14 days in a row. Then you fill in a short production access form and wait for Google's review. This guide explains every part of the rule as Google states it in the Play Console Help Center, what actually trips developers up, and a realistic timeline from first upload to public release.

### Who has to do closed testing

Google's Help Center says the requirement applies to personal developer accounts created after 13 November 2023. Until those apps pass it, they are not eligible for distribution on Google Play.

If your account was created before that date, or it is an organization account (a business verified with a D-U-N-S number), the closed testing requirement does not apply to you. Each app on an affected personal account goes through the process before it gets production access.

- Personal account, created after 13 Nov 2023: closed test required.
- Personal account, created before 13 Nov 2023: not required.
- Organization account: not required, but you need a D-U-N-S number and a verified organization website. See the guide on organization vs personal accounts.

### The rule in one sentence

Run a closed test with at least 12 testers who have been opted in continuously for at least 14 days, then apply for production access from the Play Console Dashboard.

Google's wording matters. The 14 days must be consecutive. Testers who opt in, test for fewer than 14 days and then opt out do not count. And at least 12 testers must still be opted in on the day you apply.

The number was 20 testers until December 2024, when Google lowered it to 12. The 14 days did not change.

### What counts as a tester

- A real Google Account that opted in. Being on your email list or in your Google Group is not enough. Each person has to open the opt-in link and tap to become a tester.
- On the closed track. People who opted into your internal test are not eligible for closed tests until they leave the internal test. Internal testing does not count toward the requirement.
- Opted in the whole time. If someone leaves and rejoins, their consecutive count starts again.
- Using the app. Google does not publish a minimum number of opens, but the production form asks how testers engaged and whether usage matched what you expect in production. Testers who install once and disappear are the main reason applications fail.

### A realistic timeline

1. Day 0: create the closed track, add testers (an email list or a Google Group), upload an app bundle and send the release for review.
2. Hours to a few days later: the release is published and the opt-in link works. Google notes the first test link can take several hours to become available.
3. Days 1 to 14: at least 12 testers stay opted in and use the app. Ship at least one update based on their feedback.
4. Day 15 or later: click Apply for production on the Dashboard and answer the questions.
5. About a week later: Google says the review usually takes seven days or less, but can occasionally take longer. You get an email when it's done.
6. After approval: the Production page unlocks. Your first production release still goes through normal app review.

Plan for roughly three to four weeks from your first closed-test upload to a public listing, if nothing goes wrong.

### The production access form

Google's form has three parts. Part one is about your closed test: how easy it was to recruit testers, how they engaged, and a summary of their feedback and how you collected it. Part two is about your app: target audience, what value it gives users, and how many installs you expect in the first year. Part three is about production readiness: what you changed after the test and how you decided the app was ready.

Write the answers before you open the form. Google warns that your answers are lost if you leave the page before clicking Next or Apply. Our guide to the production access questions and the free answer tool at https://testerexchange.com/tools/production-answers/ help you draft them from real numbers.

### Why apps don't pass

Google's Help Center lists two reasons you may need to keep running your closed test: fewer than 12 opted-in testers, or not enough engagement from testers. In practice developers hit these problems:

- Asking exactly 12 people. One dropout on day 10 and you are at 11.
- Testers who install and never open the app again.
- Many accounts on one phone, or accounts that are not real people.
- No updates and no feedback during the 14 days, so there is nothing to describe in the form.
- Short, generic answers in the questionnaire.

If you already got a "more testing required" reply, read the guide on insufficient testing engagement and the guide on what to do when production access is rejected.

### Where to get 12 testers

Google does not say where testers must come from. Friends and family work if you know enough Android users who will open your app daily for two weeks. Test-for-test communities are free but need your time. Paid services are faster.

Tester Exchange does both. Pay once ($12.99 for 12 testers, $14.99 for 15, $22.99 for 25), or get testers free by testing other developers' apps at https://testerexchange.com/earn in your Android phone's browser. Every tester is a real person on their own phone, and you see daily use for each one. We recommend 15 testers so a dropout or two can't push you under 12.

### Frequently asked questions

**Is it 12 or 20 testers?** 12. Google lowered it from 20 to 12 in December 2024. The 14 continuous days stayed the same.

**Does the requirement apply to my old account?** Only personal accounts created after 13 November 2023 must run the closed test. Older personal accounts and organization accounts are not covered by it.

**Do I need to repeat closed testing for every app?** Production access is granted per app on affected personal accounts, so plan a closed test for each new app.

**Does internal testing count?** No. It has to be a closed test. Google also says people opted into your internal test can't join your closed test until they leave the internal one.

**Do testers have to use the app every day?** Google doesn't publish a minimum. It asks about engagement in the production form, so regular real use by most testers is the safest pattern.

**How long does Google take to review production access?** Google says usually seven days or less, but it can occasionally take longer.

## After the 14 days: production access review time and your first release
URL: https://testerexchange.com/guide/google-play-review-time-after-closed-testing/

Your closed test has had at least 12 testers opted in for 14 days in a row. The Apply for production button is waiting. What happens next, and how long until your app is actually on Google Play? There are two separate waits: Google's review of your production access application, then the normal review of your first production release. This guide walks through both, using Google's Help Center for the official parts.

### Before you click Apply

- At least 12 testers are opted in right now. Google requires this on the day you apply, not just at some point.
- Those testers have been opted in for at least 14 consecutive days.
- Testers actually used the app, and you can describe how.
- You have feedback to summarize and at least one change you made because of it.
- Your App content declarations, store listing and Policy status have no open issues.

Don't close the closed test or remove testers when you apply. If Google wants more testing, you'll need them.

### Applying for production access

1. Open Play Console and go to your app's Dashboard.
2. Click Apply for production. Google shows this once the closed testing requirement is met.
3. Answer the three parts: about your closed test (recruiting, engagement, feedback), about your app (audience, value, expected installs in year one) and about production readiness (what you changed and how you know it's ready).
4. Click Apply. Google warns that answers are lost if you leave the page before Next or Apply, so draft them elsewhere first.

The guide on production access questions explains each question, and the free tool at https://testerexchange.com/tools/production-answers/ drafts answers from your real numbers.

### How long the review takes

Google's Help Center says the review of a production access application usually takes seven days or less, but can occasionally take longer. The account owner gets an email when the review is complete.

Google doesn't publish a way to speed this up. Waiting a few extra days past a week is not unusual, and contacting support usually won't change the timing. Use the time to keep testing and fixing bugs; testers stay on your closed track.

### The two possible outcomes

- Approved: you can access the Production page and publish your app on Google Play. Open testing also becomes available.
- More testing needed: Google says you may need to continue running your closed test, for example if you had fewer than 12 opted-in testers or not enough engagement. See the guide on what to do when production access is rejected.

### Your first production release

Production access is not the same as being live. You still need to create a production release, and it goes through Google's normal app review like any other app. Google doesn't promise a fixed time for this review. New apps from new accounts often take longer than updates from established ones, so allow several days and plan your launch date with margin.

1. Go to Test and release, then Production, then Create new release.
2. Promote the build from your closed track, or upload a new .aab. Using the build your testers already ran is the safer choice.
3. Write release notes and choose countries.
4. Consider a staged rollout (for example 20% of users) so you can catch problems early.
5. Send the changes for review in Publishing overview. If managed publishing is on, click Publish after approval to go live when you choose.
6. Once approved and published, the app can take a little while to appear in Play Store search. Share the direct link in the meantime.

### Full timeline from the first upload

- Closed track setup and first review: hours to a few days.
- Closed test: at least 14 days once 12 testers are opted in.
- Production access review: usually seven days or less, according to Google.
- First production release review: often a few days; can be longer.
- Total: plan on about four weeks from first closed-test upload to public listing, and more if anything needs fixing.

### After launch

Google advises continuing to test your app before publishing production updates. Keep the closed track as a beta channel for your early testers, and consider open testing for a larger audience.

If you haven't reached day 14 yet, the biggest time saver is starting with enough testers. Tester Exchange sends real people on their own Android phones: $12.99 for 12, $14.99 for 15 or $22.99 for 25, paid once, or free if you test other developers' apps at https://testerexchange.com/earn. We recommend 15 so a dropout can't push you under 12 right before you apply.

### Frequently asked questions

**How long does Google take to approve production access?** Google says the review usually takes seven days or less, but can occasionally take longer.

**Is my app live once production access is approved?** No. You still create a production release, which goes through normal app review before it's published.

**Can testers leave once I've applied?** Keep them until you're approved. Google requires at least 12 opted-in testers when you apply, and you may need to continue the test.

**Why is the Apply for production button missing?** It appears once you meet the requirement: at least 12 testers opted in continuously for 14 days. Check the Dashboard for your current count.

**Can I speed up the review?** Google doesn't offer a way to. Make sure there are no policy or declaration issues so the review isn't held up.
